questions.title: Why did the panel order vacate the March 25, 2025 stay and issue a new stay pending appeal instead?
questions.question_body: I'm trying to chart the procedural history of the stay in this case. The panel issued a stay on March 25, then another on April 21, May 9, and then July 18. The latest order on September 12 vacates all of those prior stays before announcing a new stay pending final resolution. Why did the court decide to clear the deck on the stay orders and machinery rather than just letting the first one stand? Does this change the practical effect of the injunction?

questions.title: How does the "likely to succeed on the merits" factor apply when the Court splits on the two different statutory challenges?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that the government is likely to succeed on the challenge to Executive Order 14163 (refugee admission suspension) but is *not* likely to succeed on the challenge regarding the defunding of USRAP under the APA. Since the standards for issuing a stay (Nken factors) weigh heavily on the showing of success on the merits, how did the panel balance these contradictory likelihoods to justify staying the District Court's introductory injunctions in their entirety?

questions.title: Can someone explain the statutory interpretation of 8 U.S.C. § 1522—specifically how to reconcile "shall" with "Authorization"?
questions.question_body: There seems to be a massive split between the majority and the dissent (Judge Lee) regarding Section 1522 of the INA. The majority reads the language requiring services as mandatory, while the dissent argues the title "Authorization for programs" and the use of "authorized" in subsections (b)-(e) make it permissive. How does the majority's reliance on "shall" in subsection (a) overcome the dissent's argument about subsections (b)-(e) using "authorized"? Does "authorization" inherently mean it's discretionary for funding purposes?

questions.title: Why does the panel direct the reinstatement of cooperative agreements in a "Stay Order" rather than an opinion on the merits?
questions.question_body: The court states that an opinion will issue on the merits in due course. However, in this interim order, it directs the government to reinstate cooperative agreements necessary to provide reception and placement services. Why is the court issuing substantive mandates on statutory obligations within a Stay Order? Does this not constitute a ruling on the merits that should wait for the formal opinion, or does the stay mechanism allow for this specific clarification now?

questions.title: What is the practical legal effect of the March 25, 2025 "limited carveout" now that the March 25 stay is vacated?
questions.question_body: In the March 25 order, the panel established a carveout for individuals "conditionally approved for refugee status" before January 20, 2025. The current September 12 order says they "vacate our prior stay issued March 25." Does this mean the carveout is still in effect for those individuals, or does vacating the March 25 stay imply that *those* individuals are now subject to the suspension like everyone else? Who has the burden of determining current status?

questions.title: How does the phrase "to the extent of available appropriations" factor into the court's decision regarding the $800 million funding reduction?
questions.question_body: The majority mentions that FY 2025 appropriated funds were reduced by $800 million in the Rescissions Act of 2025. However, the court also mentions that the funding language in § 1522 uses "to the extent of available appropriations." If Congress has cut the funding, does that Bankruptcy Act/Reduced Funding mean the Secretary is explicitly released from the § 1522 duty in the year of the reduction? Or can the court require reinstatement of agreements regardless of whether the money exists in the account?

questions.title: Why does the court cite Trump v. Hawaii to defer to the President on § 1182(f) but seemingly deny deference on the APA challenge to funding?
questions.question_body: The opinion relies on Trump v. Hawaii to establish that the President has broad discretion under § 1182(f) to suspend entry. However, it simultaneously concludes the Government is not likely to prevail on the APA/Funding challenge by pointing to specific mandatory language of § 1522. Is there a doctrinal limit to how far the Trump deference command extends? Did the court find that the "detrimental to the interests" finding doesn't cover the domestic statutory obligations of § 1522, or does it violate the Refugee Act's intent?
